parts.title: Part I – Multiple Choice Questions
parts.instructions: Part I contains 80 questions. You must answer all of them. Each question carries 1 point. There is only one best answer for each question; blacken the letter of your choice on the SCANTRON answer sheet with a pencil. (The paper has no printed section headings; items 1–40 are mostly Economics and 41–80 mostly Accounting – shown in each question's 'section' field; item 21 (cost of goods sold) is tagged Accounting and item 42 (balance of trade) Economics.)

parts.title: Part II – Work Out and Short Answer Questions
parts.instructions: Part II contains seven work out and short answer questions. You must answer all of them. This part carries twenty points. Write your answers on the separate answer sheet provided.

questions.stem: Economics is the study of how

options.A: to fully satisfy our unlimited wants.
options.C: to reduce our wants until we are satisfied.
options.D: to avoid having to make trade-offs.
options.E: society manages its limited wants and unlimited resources.

explanation_steps: Textbook: economics studies how individuals and societies choose to use scarce resources to satisfy unlimited wants.
Wants can never be fully satisfied (A), scarcity forces trade-offs (D), and E reverses ‘limited’ and ‘unlimited’. Answer: B.
tips: Scarce resources + unlimited wants – watch for options that swap the two adjectives.

similar_questions.stem: Scarcity means that

options.A: resources are limited relative to wants

explanation_steps: Answer: A.

questions.stem: The three essential economic systems used to solve central economic questions are
explanation_steps: Economic systems answer what, how and for whom to produce. The textbook lists traditional, command (planned), market (free enterprise) and mixed economies.
Of the options only C lists economic systems (B = economic agents, E = factors of production). Answer: C.
tips: Don’t confuse economic systems with economic agents (households, firms, government) or factors of production.

similar_questions.stem: An economy in which the government owns most resources and decides what to produce is a
explanation_steps: Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: The textbook also names the traditional economy (four systems); C is the only option that lists economic systems.

questions.stem: The production possibility curve (PPC) shows

options.A: the maximum amount of resources that an economy possesses.
options.B: the maximum amount of two goods that an economy can produce with fixed resources.
options.C: the unlimited resources of an economy.
options.D: all of the goods an economy can produce while leaving some resources idle.
options.E: the maximum amount of goods an economy can consume.

explanation_steps: A PPC shows the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce when resources and technology are fixed and fully used.
Idle resources give points INSIDE the curve (D). Answer: B.
tips: On the PPC = efficient (full use); inside = unemployment/inefficiency; outside = unattainable.

similar_questions.stem: A point outside the PPC is

options.D: the same as a point on the curve

explanation_steps: Answer: C.

explanation_steps: A capital good is a man-made good used to produce other goods and services (machines, tools, buildings).
The machine is not used up in one cup and is not consumed. Answer: D.
tips: Capital goods produce other goods; intermediate goods (flour, cloth) become part of other goods.

explanation_steps: Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements <u>is correct</u>?

options.A: Limited liability is an advantage of a corporation.
options.B: Unlimited liability is an advantage of a partnership.
options.C: Retention of profit is a disadvantage of a sole proprietorship.
options.D: Double taxation is an advantage of a corporation.
options.E: Unlimited liability is an advantage of a sole proprietorship.

explanation_steps: Shareholders of a corporation can lose only what they invested – limited liability is its main advantage.

Unlimited liability is a DISADVANTAGE of sole proprietorships and partnerships; keeping all profit is an ADVANTAGE of a sole proprietorship; double taxation is a DISADVANTAGE of a corporation. Answer: A.
tips: Check each statement for a swapped ‘advantage/disadvantage’.

similar_questions.stem: A disadvantage of a sole proprietorship is
explanation_steps: Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements <u>is not</u> correct?
explanation_steps: Transport links regions and people; it breaks isolation rather than facilitating it.
A, B, D and E are listed as importance of transport. Answer: C.
tips: Look for the word that reverses a known benefit (isolation ↔ integration).

similar_questions.stem: Which is NOT a benefit of good communication networks?
explanation_steps: Answer: C.

questions.stem: The one that distinguishes money from other assets is its function as a
explanation_steps: Other assets (land, gold, shares) can also store value, but only money is generally accepted in exchange for goods and services.
The medium-of-exchange function is the primary function that makes money ‘money’. Answer: A.
tips: Store of value is shared with many assets; medium of exchange is unique to money.

similar_questions.stem: Money removes the problem of double coincidence of wants because it serves as a
explanation_steps: Answer: B.

questions.stem: All of the following are necessary criteria for a commodity to function as money <u>except</u> that it must
explanation_steps: Good money must be durable, acceptable, portable, divisible and hard to counterfeit (among others).
Deteriorating quickly is the opposite of durability. Answer: A.
tips: Qualities of money: durable, portable, divisible, acceptable, homogeneous, scarce/hard to imitate, stable in value.

similar_questions.stem: Which is a desirable quality of money?
explanation_steps: Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following are the primary liabilities of a commercial bank?
explanation_steps: A commercial bank accepts deposits from the public and must repay them on demand or at maturity – deposits are what the bank OWES.
Loans, mortgages and securities it holds are its assets. Answer: D.
tips: For a bank: deposits = liabilities; loans = assets.

similar_questions.stem: For a commercial bank, loans given to customers are
explanation_steps: Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following <u>is not</u> a function of the Bank of Eritrea?

options.A: Acts as lender of last resort

explanation_steps: The central bank ‘generally does not deal directly with the public; it deals with the public only indirectly through the commercial banks’ (G10 p.45).
Accepting deposits from and lending to the public is a commercial-bank function. The other four are central-bank functions. Answer: C.
tips: Central bank = banker to government and banks; commercial banks = deposits and loans for the public.

similar_questions.stem: Which is a function of a central bank?

options.C: giving car loans to the public

explanation_steps: Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: The paper says ‘Bank of Eritrea’ here and ‘National Bank of Eritrea’ in item 40 (same institution).

questions.stem: In a perfect competition, each individual seller faces _____ demand curve.
explanation_steps: A perfectly competitive firm is a price taker: it can sell any quantity at the market price, so its demand curve is horizontal (perfectly elastic) at that price.
Answer: A.
tips: Firm in perfect competition: horizontal demand (P = MR = AR); the MARKET demand still slopes downward.

similar_questions.stem: A price taker is a firm that
explanation_steps: Answer: B.

questions.stem: For perfect competition to exist there must be

options.C: restrictions to the entry of new firms.

explanation_steps: Conditions: many buyers and sellers, homogeneous (identical) products, free entry and exit, perfect mobility of resources, perfect information.
Answer: E.
tips: Every wrong option here is the opposite of a perfect-competition condition.

similar_questions.stem: Which is a feature of perfect competition?
explanation_steps: Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following <u>will not</u> cause a change in the demand for coffee?

options.A: Decrease in the price of milk which is a complement to coffee
options.B: An increase in the price of coffee
options.C: An increase in the number of people drinking coffee
options.D: An increase in the income of consumers
options.E: A decrease in the price of tea which is a substitute to coffee

explanation_steps: A change in the good’s OWN price causes a movement along the demand curve (change in quantity demanded), not a change (shift) in demand.
Prices of complements/substitutes, number of buyers and income shift the demand curve. Answer: B.
tips: Own price → change in quantity demanded; any other determinant → change in demand.

similar_questions.stem: A shift of the demand curve for tea is caused by

options.A: a fall in the price of tea
options.C: a rise in the price of tea

explanation_steps: Answer: B.

questions.stem: If farmers decide to plant more cabbage next year, ceteris paribus, the

options.A: supply curve for cabbage next year will shift to the left.
options.B: demand curve for cabbage this year will shift to the right.
options.C: supply curve for cabbage next year will be horizontal.
options.D: supply curve for cabbage next year will shift to the right.
options.E: demand curve for cabbage this year will shift to the left.

explanation_steps: More cabbage planted = more cabbage offered at every price next year → supply increases → supply curve shifts right.
Demand is not affected. Answer: D.
tips: More sellers or more planting → supply shifts right; demand concerns buyers.

similar_questions.stem: A drought destroys much of the wheat crop. The supply curve of wheat will
explanation_steps: Answer: B.

questions.stem: At price P₃ in the Figure 1 below, [Figure 1 (demand and supply): D and S intersect at P₂, Q₂. At price P₃: quantity demanded = Q₁, quantity supplied = Q₄. At price P₁: quantity supplied = Q₁, quantity demanded = Q₃.]
questions.image_alt: Figure 1. Demand and Supply curves: Price on the vertical axis (P₁ < P₂ < P₃), Quantity on the horizontal axis (Q₁ < Q₂ < Q₃ < Q₄). Downward-sloping D and upward-sloping S cross at (Q₂, P₂). At P₃ the dashed line meets D above Q₁ and S above Q₄. At P₁ it meets S above Q₁ and D above Q₃.

options.B: there will be a surplus of Q₄ – Q₁.
options.C: there will be a tendency for prices to rise.
options.E: there will be a shortage of Q₄ – Q₁

explanation_steps: P₃ is above the equilibrium price P₂. At P₃, buyers want Q₁ (on D) and sellers offer Q₄ (on S).
Qs > Qd → surplus = Q₄ − Q₁; prices will tend to FALL. Answer: B.
tips: Above equilibrium → surplus and falling price; below → shortage and rising price.

similar_questions.stem: In the same figure, what happens at price P₁?
explanation_steps: At P₁: Qs = Q₁, Qd = Q₃ → shortage Q₃ − Q₁. Answer: B.

questions.stem: When demand is ________, a decrease in price ________ total revenue.
explanation_steps: Inelastic demand: quantity rises by a smaller % than price falls → TR = P × Q falls.
Elastic: price cut raises TR; unit elastic: TR unchanged. Only E is consistent. Answer: E.
tips: Inelastic: P and TR move in the same direction; elastic: opposite directions; unit elastic: TR constant.

similar_questions.stem: When demand is elastic, a price increase will
explanation_steps: Answer: B.

questions.stem: What will happen to equilibrium price and quantity, if supply increases and demand remains unchanged?

options.A: Equilibrium price increases and equilibrium quantity decreases.
options.B: Equilibrium price decreases and equilibrium quantity decreases.
options.C: Equilibrium price decreases and equilibrium quantity increases.
options.D: Equilibrium price increases and equilibrium quantity increases.
options.E: Equilibrium price increases and equilibrium quantity remains unchanged.

explanation_steps: Supply shifts right along an unchanged downward-sloping demand curve: the new intersection is lower and further right.
Price falls, quantity rises. Answer: C.
tips: Sketch the shift – never answer shift questions from memory alone.

similar_questions.stem: If demand increases and supply is unchanged, equilibrium
explanation_steps: Answer: A.

questions.stem: Which of the following goods is most likely to have high price elasticity of demand?

options.A: A good for which there are many close substitutes
options.B: A good that forms a very small part of a person’s total budget
options.E: A good which is broadly defined

explanation_steps: Many close substitutes let buyers switch easily when the price rises → demand is elastic.
Small budget share, necessities (staple food, medicine) and broadly defined goods have inelastic demand. Answer: A.
tips: Determinants of elasticity: substitutes, necessity vs luxury, budget share, time, definition of the good.

similar_questions.stem: Demand for salt is inelastic mainly because

options.B: it takes a tiny share of income

explanation_steps: Answer: B.

questions.stem: The price elasticity of demand for furniture is estimated at -1.3. This value indicates a one percent increase in the

options.A: price of furniture will increase the quantity of furniture demanded by 1.3 percent.
options.B: price of furniture will decrease the quantity of furniture demanded by 1.3 percent.
options.C: quantity of furniture demanded will decrease the price of furniture by 1.3 percent.
options.D: quantity of furniture demanded will increase the price of furniture by 1.3 percent.
options.E: price of furniture will decrease the quantity of furniture demanded by 13 percent.

explanation_steps: A 1% price rise lowers quantity demanded by 1.3%. Answer: B.
tips: The coefficient tells the % change in QUANTITY for a 1% change in PRICE; the minus sign means opposite directions.

questions.stem: Along a downward sloping demand curve for a good, the price elasticity of demand will increase the

options.A: higher the price of the good.
options.B: higher the price of other related goods.
options.C: higher the income level of consumers.
options.D: lower the price of the good.
options.E: higher the quantity of the good.

explanation_steps: On a straight-line demand curve the slope ΔQ/ΔP is constant, so |Ped| = (ΔQ/ΔP) × (P/Q) grows as P rises and Q falls.
Demand is elastic at the upper (high-price) end and inelastic at the lower end. Answer: A.
tips: Top of a linear demand curve = elastic; bottom = inelastic; midpoint = unit elastic.

similar_questions.stem: On a linear demand curve, demand is unit elastic at
explanation_steps: Answer: B.

textbook_ref.note: The G11 book gives Ped = (ΔQ/Q₁) ÷ (ΔP/P₁) (p.25) but does not state explicitly how Ped varies along a linear curve; the result follows from the formula.

questions.review_flag: Textbook gap: variation of elasticity along a linear demand curve is not stated explicitly in the G11 book; the key follows from the textbook formula (standard economics).

explanation_steps: COGS = beginning inventory + cost of goods purchased − ending inventory.
tips: Goods available for sale (414,000, option D) minus ending inventory = COGS.

questions.stem: Based on Table 1 below, what is the average cost of producing 4 units?
explanation_steps: Total cost at 4 units = FC + VC = 100 + 700 = 800.
Average (total) cost = TC ÷ Q = 800 ÷ 4 = 200. Answer: E.
tips: ‘Average cost’ without qualification = average TOTAL cost; AVC (175) and AFC (25) are traps.

similar_questions.stem: FC = 200 and VC = 1,000 at 4 units. Average cost = ?

questions.stem: Based on Table 1 above, what is the marginal cost of the third unit?
explanation_steps: MC = change in total cost = TC₃ − TC₂ = (100 + 350) − (100 + 300) = 450 − 400 = 50.
(Fixed cost does not change, so MC = ΔVC = 350 − 300.) Answer: C.
tips: MC depends only on variable cost changes.

questions.stem: In economics, the short run is a period of time

options.B: in which all inputs are variable.
options.C: in which all inputs are fixed.
options.D: in which the quantity of at least one input is fixed and the quantities of the other inputs can be varied.
options.E: in which all inputs are variable but technology is fixed.

explanation_steps: Short run: at least one factor (e.g. plant size) is fixed; long run: all factors variable.
It is not a calendar length. Answer: D.
tips: Short run/long run are defined by fixed inputs, not months.

similar_questions.stem: The long run is a period in which

options.B: at least one input is fixed

explanation_steps: Answer: A.

questions.stem: The behavior of U-shaped cost curves implies that costs

options.A: first rise, reach maximum and then fall.
options.B: are fixed and do not change in the long run.
options.D: never rise once they reach minimum.
options.E: first fall, reach minimum and then rise.

explanation_steps: AVC, ATC and MC are U-shaped: they fall at first (increasing returns), reach a minimum and then rise (diminishing returns).
Answer: E.
tips: U shape = down, minimum, up.

similar_questions.stem: The rising part of the short-run MC curve is explained by
explanation_steps: Answer: B.

questions.stem: Utility from consuming a good is understood to mean, how

options.B: much satisfaction we get from consuming a good.
options.C: much it costs to buy the good.
options.E: much profit we get from the good.

explanation_steps: Utility = the satisfaction a consumer gets from consuming a good or service.
Answer: B.
tips: Utility is satisfaction, not usefulness or price.

similar_questions.stem: Total utility is

options.A: the satisfaction from all units consumed
options.B: the extra satisfaction from one more unit

explanation_steps: Answer: A.

questions.stem: The total utility gained from consuming additional units of a good will increase if the

options.A: the opportunity cost of consuming rises.

explanation_steps: MU = ΔTU; TU rises while MU > 0, is at its maximum when MU = 0, and falls when MU < 0.
Answer: C.
tips: MU positive → TU rising; MU zero → TU maximum; MU negative → TU falling.

similar_questions.stem: Total utility is at its maximum when marginal utility is
explanation_steps: Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which one of the following statements <u>is incorrect</u>?

options.A: The closer to the origin an indifference curve lies, the greater the level of satisfaction indicated by the curve.
options.B: For any two goods or services, each consumer has various indifference curves, which provide the consumer a particular level of satisfaction.
options.C: For each consumer we may construct an indifference map, which consists of a collection of indifference curves.
options.D: Indifference curves never intersect each other.
options.E: Indifference curves never touch each other.

explanation_steps: Higher indifference curves (further from the origin) represent MORE of both goods and therefore greater satisfaction; curves closer to the origin mean LESS satisfaction.
B, C, D (and E) are standard properties. Answer: A.
tips: Further from the origin = higher satisfaction.

similar_questions.stem: Which is a property of indifference curves?
explanation_steps: Answer: C.

questions.stem: The total value of all final goods and services produced in a country during a particular year is called the
explanation_steps: GDP = market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a given period (usually a year).
Answer: C.
tips: Domestic = produced inside the country; National = produced by the country’s citizens anywhere.

similar_questions.stem: GNP differs from GDP by
explanation_steps: GNP = GDP + net factor income from abroad. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The Gross Domestic Product of a country can be estimated by calculating the

options.C: surplus of government current revenue over current expenditure.
options.D: surplus on the current account of the balance of payments.
options.E: total of all capital consumption allowances.

explanation_steps: Income approach: GDP is measured by adding all factor incomes (wages, rent, interest, profit) earned in producing output (with adjustments for depreciation and indirect taxes).
Profits alone (B) are only one factor income. Answer: A.
tips: Three methods: income (factor incomes), expenditure (C + I + G + X − M) and value added (product).

similar_questions.stem: Adding C + I + G + (X − M) measures GDP by the
explanation_steps: Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a component of investment?
explanation_steps: Investment (I) in national accounts = spending on NEW capital goods (machinery, buildings) and additions to inventories.
A pizza is consumption; second-hand goods were counted when first produced. Answer: A.
tips: Investment = new capital goods; buying used assets or shares is not investment in GDP.

similar_questions.stem: Which is counted as investment in GDP?

options.B: a firm building a new warehouse

explanation_steps: Answer: B.

questions.stem: The major source of government revenue is
explanation_steps: Taxes (direct and indirect) are the main source of government revenue; grants, fines, borrowing and money creation are minor or undesirable sources.
Answer: B.
tips: Tax revenue dominates government income in almost every country.

similar_questions.stem: A tax on income is a
explanation_steps: Answer: A.

questions.stem: The three ways of calculating GDP are

options.A: value added, price and income methods.
options.C: expenditure, spending and value added methods.
options.D: income, expenditure and value added methods.
options.E: accounting, finance and book keeping methods.

explanation_steps: GDP can be measured by the income approach, the expenditure approach and the value-added (product/output) approach.
C repeats expenditure = spending. Answer: D.
tips: Expenditure and spending are the same method – a trap.

similar_questions.stem: Summing the value added at each stage of production measures GDP by the
explanation_steps: Answer: C.

explanation_steps: Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following <u>is correct</u>?

options.D: GDP includes future prices of goods and services.

explanation_steps: GDP counts only final goods produced in the current period at market value.

tips: Excluded from GDP: intermediate goods, second-hand sales, transfer payments, financial transactions, non-market activities.

similar_questions.stem: Which is excluded from GDP?

options.C: the resale of a used house

explanation_steps: Answer: C.

explanation_steps: Progressive tax: the tax RATE rises as income rises (e.g. the Eritrean income tax table 2% → 30%).
Proportional = same rate; regressive = lower rate for the rich. Answer: E.
tips: Eritrea’s employment income tax (2%, 10%, 20%, 25%, 30%) is a progressive tax.

explanation_steps: Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of positive externality?
explanation_steps: A positive externality is a benefit to third parties: vaccinating one child also protects others from infection.
The other options are negative externalities (costs imposed on others). Answer: C.
tips: Externality = effect on a third party; positive = benefit, negative = cost.

similar_questions.stem: A factory dumping waste into a river creates a
explanation_steps: Answer: B.

questions.stem: According to the concept of comparative advantage, specialization and trade between two countries will benefit

options.A: only the country with the lowest labor costs.
options.B: both countries, provided neither country has an absolute advantage in both goods.
options.C: both countries, provided domestic opportunity costs differ in the two countries.
options.D: only the country with the highest tariff rate.

explanation_steps: Comparative advantage depends on opportunity costs: if they differ, each country specialises in the good with the lower opportunity cost and both gain.
Gains exist even if one country has an absolute advantage in both goods, so B is wrong. Answer: C.
tips: Comparative advantage = lower OPPORTUNITY cost, not lower absolute cost.

explanation_steps: X: 1 shirt costs 0.5 radio; Y: 1 shirt costs 1 radio → X in shirts. Answer: B.

explanation_steps: A fixed (pegged) exchange rate is set by the central bank/government rather than by market forces.

options.A: the value of all exports and imports of a country.

explanation_steps: Answer: B.

questions.stem: Lidya works in Barka canned Food factory. She is paid on hourly basis. During normal working hours, which are 178 hours per month, she is paid 8 Nakfa per hour. questions.stem: Name three non-price determinants of demand for an individual consumer. (3 points)
questions.answer: Any three of: (1) the consumer’s income; (2) prices of related goods (substitutes and complements); (3) tastes and preferences; (4) expectations about future prices (and income).
explanation_steps: The price of the good itself changes only the QUANTITY demanded; the other factors shift the demand curve.
G11 textbook: ‘These factors are income, price of related goods, tastes and preferences, expectations on future price of the commodity demanded, and size of population.’
Size of population / number of buyers affects MARKET demand, not an individual consumer’s demand – better to avoid it here.
marking_points: 1 point for each correct determinant (maximum 3): income; prices of related goods (substitutes/complements); tastes and preferences; expectations.
Number of buyers/population may be accepted by some markers but it is a market-demand determinant.
tips: ‘Non-price’ means: do NOT write ‘price of the good’.

similar_questions.stem: Name two non-price determinants of supply.
similar_questions.answer: Any two of: cost of inputs, technology, prices of related goods in production, number of sellers, expectations, taxes/subsidies, weather.
explanation_steps: Own price moves along the supply curve; the others shift it.

questions.stem: ________ is the major determinant of household consumption. (1 point)
explanation_steps: G12 p.14: aggregate consumption is basically determined by the disposable personal income received by households; the consumption function is C = f(Yd).
The higher the disposable income, the higher the consumption, other things equal.
tips: ‘Income’ alone is usually accepted, but ‘disposable income’ is the textbook answer.

similar_questions.stem: ________ is the part of disposable income that is not consumed.
explanation_steps: Yd = C + S → S = Yd − C.

questions.stem: ________ is the major source of government revenue. (1 point)

tips: Same idea as MCQ 33.

explanation_steps: An indirect tax on imports.

questions.stem:
In recent years, Golden Plate Pizzeria purchased two delivery motor cycles. The two motor cycles are depreciated using different methods as given in the table. For the units-of-activity method (motor cycle #2), total life in terms of kilometres is expected to be 120,000. Actual kilometres of use in the first two years were: 2010 – 34,000; 2011 – 30,000.
A. Compute the amount of depreciation expense on motor cycle #1 at December 31, 2011. (1 point)
B. Compute the amount of accumulated depreciation on motor cycle #1 at December 31, 2011. (1 point)
C. Compute the amount of depreciation expense on motor cycle #2 at December 31, 2010. (1 point)
D. Compute the amount of depreciation expense on motor cycle #2 at December 31, 2011. (1 point)
E. Compute the amount of accumulated depreciation on motor cycle #2 at December 31, 2011. (1 point)

stem_tables.title: Golden Plate Pizzeria – delivery motor cycles (as printed)

explanation_steps: #1 straight-line: (cost − salvage) ÷ life = (96,000 − 6,000) ÷ 5 = 18,000 per year → 2011 expense 18,000.
Accumulated depreciation 31 Dec 2011 = 4 full years (2008, 2009, 2010, 2011) × 18,000 = 72,000.
#2 units of activity: rate = (80,000 − 8,000) ÷ 120,000 km = 0.60 per km.
tips: Straight-line: the same amount every year – count the years carefully from the purchase date.
Units of activity: compute the rate per km first.

questions.stem:
In order to produce equal adjusted balances for Huda Laundry, appropriate action need to be taken for the statements given in Column A. From the actions listed below from (a) to (f), name the <u>appropriate</u> action for each statement. (5 points)
Actions: a) Added to the bank statement balance; b) Deducted from the bank statement balance; c) Added to the depositor’s balance; d) Deducted from the depositor’s balance; e) Exempted from the bank reconciliation statement; f) No action is needed.
7.1 Statement includes a credit memorandum, representing the collection of the proceeds of a notes receivable by the bank on behalf of Huda Laundry.
7.2 Deposits in transit.
7.3 Seven outstanding checks were not recorded on the statement.
7.4 A customer’s check that Huda Laundry had deposited was returned with “nonsufficient funds” stamped across the face.
7.5 A $96 check was erroneously recorded in Huda Laundry check stubs as $69.

subparts.question: Deposits in transit
subparts.answer: (a) Added to the bank statement balance

subparts.question: Outstanding checks
subparts.answer: (b) Deducted from the bank statement balance
steps: Books recorded; bank has not paid.

answer_tables.title: Huda Laundry – reconciling actions
rows: The bank has added it; the books have not yet.
(a) Added to the bank statement balance
Recorded in the books, not yet by the bank.
(b) Deducted from the bank statement balance
Recorded in the books, not yet paid by the bank.
The bank has deducted it; the books still show it as cash.
The books understate the payment by 96 − 69 = 27.

explanation_steps: Bank side: items the bank has not yet recorded – deposits in transit are ADDED (a), outstanding checks are DEDUCTED (b).
Book side: items the bank recorded but the books did not – collection of a note is ADDED (c); an NSF check is DEDUCTED (d).
Depositor’s error: a payment of 96 recorded as 69 understates payments by 27 → deduct 27 from the depositor’s balance (d).
tips: Ask: who has NOT yet recorded the item – the bank or the business? Adjust that side.

similar_questions.stem: In a bank reconciliation, where do bank service charges of 50 go?
explanation_steps: The bank has already deducted them; the books have not.
